content.text: Students build from finalized research, discussion, drafting, peer review, and revision to complete a polished explanation of a hidden innovator’s contribution.
Credible writing comes from clear ideas, strong evidence, and accurate sources.
Students will polish presentation delivery and share their findings with visuals and formal style.
Today’s work helps students finalize the informative research essay, the argument paragraph, the bibliography, and the evidence they will use in presentation.

Turn and Talk
Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the question.
What makes a final draft feel complete instead of just unfinished writing with fewer mistakes?
Sentence Combining

Sometimes writers drop a quotation or fact into a paragraph without introducing it. That is called quote dropping. It can make the paragraph feel choppy because the evidence is not connected to the writer’s own sentence. Let’s fix that by combining ideas so the source, the year, and the evidence work together in one sentence.
Directions:
Look at these short ideas:
Margot Lee Shetterly wrote
Hidden Figures
The book was published in 2016.
Katherine Johnson’s math work helped solve major flight problems.
How could we combine these ideas into one smooth sentence using the frame “According to ___ (year), ___”?
Why is this combined sentence stronger than dropping the evidence into the paragraph by itself?

Now revise one sentence from your own draft. Find a place where you have a fact or quotation that feels dropped in. Rewrite it so the source name and year appear in the sentence using a frame like “According to ___ in [source title] (year), ___.”
What should your reader learn right away when you introduce evidence from a source?
Part A: Complete Writing
Directions:

First, use your digital draft to finalize your informative research essay and argument paragraph so your ideas are complete, clearly explained, and supported with evidence. Use keyboarding skills to complete final draft sections, revise sentences, format citations, and prepare your writing for submission or publication. Use the rubric to ensure your writing includes all necessary components.
Then, use your finished writing to prepare your presentation by selecting your strongest claim, evidence, and visual. Focus on completing the writing before moving into presentation planning.
Final Digital Draft Check:
Did I complete all required essay and argument sections?
Did I format my writing so it is easy to read?
Did I use digital tools to revise, edit, and finalize my work?
Are my citations and bibliography ready for submission?
Is my visual saved or prepared for presentation?
Reflection (W.6.4)
Reflect on your writing using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to finish your final draft with strong citations, smooth transitions, and accurate sources?
Part B: Prepare Presentation
Directions:
Say: Your presentation is not a reading of your essay. It is a short explanation of your most important ideas.
To prepare, choose:
one clear claim
one strong piece of evidence
one explanation of how your evidence supports your claim
one visual that helps your audience understand your idea
Use short, clear sentences. Your goal is to help your audience understand your idea quickly, not to include every detail.
Which claim are you most likely to present, and how do your evidence and visual work together to support it?
How is preparing for a presentation different from writing an informative research essay or argumentative paragraph?
Quick Write
Directions:

In two to three sentences, describe one final step you completed today that improved your writing or presentation preparation. Explain how this step made your work clearer, more accurate, or easier for a reader or audience to understand.

This section helps students shift into final-stage thinking by prioritizing completion and clarity. Students review expectations for a complete performance task and identify what makes writing feel finished and credible. They begin preparing to move from revision into finalization and presentation planning.
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:
Turn and talk with a partner to discuss your response to the question.
Ask:
What makes a final draft feel complete instead of just unfinished writing with fewer mistakes?

A final draft feels complete when the ideas are connected, the evidence supports the claim clearly, and the writing includes source credit. It also feels finished when the bibliography and presentation evidence are ready, not just the paragraphs.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:

Today, your priority is to finalize your writing first so it is clear, complete, accurate, and ready to share or publish digitally. After that, you will use your final ideas to prepare a strong presentation that explains your claim, evidence, and visuals more concisely and clearly.
Students reconnect to their revision work and prepare to finish drafts with stronger citation and cohesion.

This mini-lesson teaches students how to combine source information and evidence into one clear sentence so their informative research essay sounds smooth and professional. The goal is to move students away from quote dropping and toward attribution that fits naturally into their own writing.
Sentence Combining

Sometimes writers drop a quotation or fact into a paragraph without introducing it. That is called quote dropping. It can make the paragraph feel choppy because the evidence is not connected to the writer’s own sentence. Let’s fix that by combining ideas so the source, the year, and the evidence work together in one sentence.
Use a mentor example connected to
Hidden Figures
Say:
We are going to practice with ideas from
Hidden Figures
because that text shows how expert information can be woven smoothly into an informative research essay.
Display these Short Ideas:
Margot Lee Shetterly wrote Hidden Figures.
The book was published in 2016.
Dorothy Vaughan prepared her team for new computer technology.
Teach the sentence-combining move:
Say:

A strong research sentence does three jobs at once. It tells who the source is, when the source was published, and what the evidence shows. One easy frame is: According to ___ in [source title] (year), ___.
Teach:
Say:

I want to use evidence about Dorothy Vaughan, but right now my fact is standing alone: “Dorothy Vaughan prepared her team for new computer technology.” If I leave it like that, my reader does not know where the information came from. So I start by adding the source: “According to Margot Lee Shetterly in
Hidden Figures
.” Next, I add the year in parentheses right where the source is named: “According to Margot Lee Shetterly in
Hidden Figures
(2016).” Now I combine the evidence into the same sentence: “According to Margot Lee Shetterly in
Hidden Figures

(2016), Dorothy Vaughan prepared her team for new computer technology by learning new skills before the new digital computers were fully adopted by NASA.” That sounds smoother because the source is built into my sentence instead of being dropped in after the fact.
Guided practice with a second
Hidden Figures
example:
Display these short ideas:
Margot Lee Shetterly wrote Hidden Figures.
The book was published in 2016.
Katherine Johnson’s math work helped solve major flight problems.
Ask:
How could we combine these ideas into one smooth sentence using the frame “According to ___ (year), ___”?
According to Margot Lee Shetterly in
Hidden Figures
(2016), Katherine Johnson’s math work helped solve major flight problems that mattered to NASA’s space missions.
Ask:
Why is this combined sentence stronger than dropping the evidence into the paragraph by itself?
This sentence is stronger because it tells the reader exactly where the information came from before giving the evidence. It sounds smoother and makes the paragraph easier to follow.
Say these directions:

Now revise one sentence from your own draft. Find a place where you have a fact or quotation that feels dropped in. Rewrite it so the source name and year appear in the sentence using a frame like “According to ___ in [source title] (year), ___.”
Ask:
What should your reader learn right away when you introduce evidence from a source?
The reader should learn who the source is and when it was published. That way, the evidence feels trustworthy and connected to the writer’s point.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
You now have a simple way to make your informative research writing sound stronger. Next, you will use this same sentence move as you finish your final draft.
Students practice combining attribution and evidence into one complete sentence so their informative research writing clearly shows where information comes from and flows smoothly from idea to idea.
Language Focus:
Attribution frames
Source title and author naming
Year in parentheses
Explanation language that connects evidence to the claim
Before Sentence Combining (preparation step—optional)
Students underline one sentence in their draft that begins with a quotation or fact but does not yet name the source smoothly.
Prompt students to start with the source information instead of adding it at the end of the sentence.
Encourage students to read the revised sentence aloud and listen for whether it sounds like one complete idea.
"You said the fact first and then the source after it—we can say: “According to Margot Lee Shetterly in
Hidden Figures
(2016), Dorothy Vaughan prepared her team for new technology."
"You said 'I got this from my book'—we can say: According to Margot Lee Shetterly in
Hidden Figures
According to ___ in [source title] (year), ___.
In [source title] (year), ___ explains that ___.
This evidence matters because ___.
If students leave out the year → Prompt: "Go back to the source information and place the year in parentheses right after the source title."
If students still write a dropped quotation or loose fact → Prompt: "Start the sentence again with ‘According to’ and make the evidence part of that same sentence."
If students write a sentence that sounds choppy → Prompt: "Read it aloud. Where can you combine two short ideas so it sounds smoother?"
Student writes one sentence that includes the source name, year, and evidence in a single smooth structure.
Student revises a dropped quotation or fact so it is clearly connected to the paragraph’s point.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Quote Dropping

Have students put a box around one loose fact or quotation in the draft and rewrite it using “According to ___ in [source title] (year), ___.” Placing the Year: Remind students that the year belongs right after the source title or source name information. Sentence Flow: Ask students to read both versions aloud and choose the one that sounds more like a full paragraph sentence. Written Expression: Allow students to say the revised sentence aloud before writing it into the draft. Alternative Expression: Allow students to provide an oral recording of the revised sentence or use speech-to-text tools before copying the final version into the draft.
Ready for extension

Invite students to write two different attribution sentences for the same piece of evidence and decide which one creates stronger paragraph flow. Challenge students to revise two evidence sentences in the same paragraph so both the source and the explanation sound connected.
Students will learn how to smoothly integrate citations and add transitions between sections of extended writing.
Part A: Complete Writing (W.6.1, W.6.2) (15 minutes)

This section focuses on completing and finalizing student writing. Students ensure that their informative essay and argument paragraph are fully developed, clearly connected, and supported with evidence. They prioritize clarity, cohesion, and completeness before moving into presentation preparation.
Say these directions:

First, use your digital draft to finalize your informative research essay and argument paragraph so your ideas are complete, clearly explained, and supported with evidence. Use keyboarding skills to complete final draft sections, revise sentences, format citations, and prepare your writing for submission or publication. Use the rubric to ensure your writing includes all necessary components.
Then, use your finished writing to prepare your presentation by selecting your strongest claim, evidence, and visual. Focus on completing the writing before moving into presentation planning.
Final Digital Draft Check:
Did I complete all required essay and argument sections?
Did I format my writing so it is easy to read?
Did I use digital tools to revise, edit, and finalize my work?
Are my citations and bibliography ready for submission?
Is my visual saved or prepared for presentation?

By the end of this section, students should have completed final draft versions of both pieces of writing. Their work should show clear claims, supported evidence, and logical transitions that make ideas easy to follow.
Students strengthen final draft sections by connecting claims, evidence, paragraph transitions, and conclusions more clearly.
Language Focus:
Section-level transitions
Claim-evidence linkage
Conclusion language
Formal academic register
Before Modeled Writing (preparation step—optional)
Students circle the section of the draft that feels least complete before finalizing. They then revise and write the final draft.
Prompt students to revise the places that most affect the reader’s understanding.
Encourage students to reread the final sentence of one paragraph and the first sentence of the next to test cohesion.
Furthermore, ___.
In addition, ___.
However, ___.
Consequently, ___.
Overall, this contribution mattered because ___.
If students have weak transitions between body paragraphs → Prompt: “Ask whether the new paragraph adds, contrasts, or shows a result.”
If students lose focus in the conclusion → Prompt: “Restate the contribution and connect it back to the thesis.”
If students leave a claim unsupported → Prompt: “Add the strongest evidence sentence you already have in your notes or draft.”
Student completes unfinished sections of the writing.
Student improves cohesion with transitions and clear thesis connection.
Check for Understanding
Provide students with a confidence continuum (i.e., 1–5). As needed, model how to demonstrate a level of confidence using the continuum.
Reflection (W.6.1, W.6.2)
Reflect on your writing using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in your ability to finish your final draft with strong citations, smooth transitions, and accurate sources?
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Finishing Sections

Suggest students complete the most incomplete section first instead of jumping around the draft. Body Paragraph Transitions: Prompt them to write one transition sentence before adding more details. Conclusion Focus: Ask “What is the one contribution you want the reader to remember?” Alternative Expression: Allow students to orally summarize the section they are revising before writing the new sentences.
Ready for extension
Invite students to strengthen one paragraph by adding a stronger section-level transition and a more precise concluding sentence.
Part B: Prepare Presentation (W.6.8) (15 minutes)

This section prepares students to present their ideas clearly by synthesizing their writing into a short, focused explanation and preparing a visual that enhances understanding. Emphasize that Part 3 requires students to communicate their thinking clearly—not read their essay—so they must select, combine, and explain their most important ideas.
Have students place their draft, source list, Research Notes, and any visuals beside them. Direct students to Part 3: Presentation of Learning in the Performance Task.
Teach:
Say:

In your essay, you explained everything in detail. In your presentation, your job is different. You are not reading your writing—you are helping your audience quickly understand your most important idea.
If I read my essay out loud, it might sound like this:
“Dorothy Vaughan learned FORTRAN so she could help NASA transition to new computer systems. According to one source, she also trained other workers…”
That sounds like reading. It’s long, and it’s hard to follow when listening.
Instead, I want to synthesize my ideas so they are clear and easy to understand. That might sound like this:

“Dorothy Vaughan deserves recognition because she helped NASA transition to new computer technology. One key example is that she learned FORTRAN and taught it to others. This shows that her work supported the entire team. This timeline helps show when that transition happened.”
Notice what I did. I started with my claim, chose one strong example, explained it clearly, and connected my visual.
Say these directions:
Say: Your presentation is not a reading of your essay. It is a short explanation of your most important ideas.
To prepare, choose:
one clear claim
one strong piece of evidence
one explanation of how your evidence supports your claim
one visual that helps your audience understand your idea
Use short, clear sentences. Your goal is to help your audience understand your idea quickly, not to include every detail.

Provide time and materials for students to create, revise, or digitally format their visuals. You may choose to have students use presentation software, a digital slide, a chart, or another approved classroom tool to prepare the visual. Circulate and prompt: “What does your visual help your audience understand?” “How does this connect to your claim?”
Ask:
Which claim are you most likely to present, and how do your evidence and visual work together to support it?

The claim I am most likely to present is that Dorothy Vaughan’s contribution enabled NASA to adapt to major technological change. The best support is a fact from my research about her programming leadership, and the timeline visual supports that claim by showing when that transition happened.
Ask:
How is preparing for a presentation different from writing an informative research essay or argumentative paragraph?
Preparing for a presentation means choosing the most important ideas and explaining them clearly, rather than including every detail.
Ask two or three students to share quick responses.
Say:

As you prepare, focus on clarity. Your goal is to help your audience understand your innovator’s contribution and why it matters using clear explanation, strong evidence, and a visual that supports your ideas.

By the end of this section, students should have a clear presentation plan that includes a claim, evidence, explanation, and visual. They should understand how to communicate complex research ideas concisely and clearly to an audience.
Students synthesize their writing into a clear claim, supporting evidence, and explanation, and prepare a visual that supports their ideas for the presentation.
Language Focus:
Claim–evidence–explanation language
Language for explaining how visuals support ideas
Formal academic language for speaking
Before Activity (preparation step—optional)
Students say one presentation claim aloud to check for clarity and focus before preparing presentation.
Encourage students to choose one claim they can clearly explain rather than summarizing their full essay.
Prompt students to select one strong piece of evidence and explain how it supports the claim.
Emphasize that the visual should help clarify the claim and explanation, not simply decorate the presentation.
Remind students they must explain both their evidence and their visual.
My claim is ___.
One example is ___.
This shows ___ because ___.
This visual supports my claim because ___.
If students choose a claim with weak support → Prompt: “Switch to the evidence point you can explain most clearly and accurately.”
If students include evidence without explanation → Prompt: “Add: ‘This shows ___ because ___.’”
If students choose a visual that does not connect tightly → Prompt: “Explain what the visual helps the audience understand about the claim.”
Student selects one clear claim and one aligned evidence point.
Student explains how the evidence supports the claim.
Student selects a visual that clearly supports the idea and explains its purpose.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Presentation Focus

Prompt students to choose one claim they can explain best rather than summarizing the whole essay. Explaining Evidence: Prompt: “Finish the sentence: ‘This shows ___ because ___.’” Visual Alignment: Ask: “What does this visual help your audience understand?” Alternative Expression: Allow students to verbally rehearse the claim–evidence–explanation–visual before writing.
Ready for extension
Invite students to prepare a second supported claim in case they want to compare two aspects of the innovator’s contribution during the presentation.
Part A: Complete Writing (W.6.1, W.6.2)
Students will finalize essay and argument sections, strengthen body-to-body and body-to-conclusion transitions, and keep claims supported with evidence.
Part B: Prepare Presentation (W.6.8)
Students will identify the claim-evidence-visual combination they will carry into presentation.

This reflection helps students identify the final steps they took to complete their performance task. Students consider how their revisions, final edits, or presentation planning improved clarity and understanding. The goal is to reinforce the connection between revision and strong communication.
Quick Write
Say these directions:

In two to three sentences, describe one final step you completed today that improved your writing or presentation preparation. Explain how this step made your work clearer, more accurate, or easier for a reader or audience to understand.

Today I finalized part of my digital draft and chose one supported claim and visual that I can use clearly in my presentation. This improved my performance task because my writing is more complete and my audience will better understand how my evidence supports my claim. This improved my performance task because it helps me explain my ideas more clearly to my audience and makes it easier for them to understand how my evidence supports my claim.
Optional Sentence Starter:
Today I ___. This improved my performance task because ___.
Students will reflect on one finalization move that improved support, cohesion, or citation clarity.

Have students complete and digitally submit or prepare their bibliography, accurately citing each source they used. Students may also finalize their presentation materials using classroom-approved digital tools.

standards.description: Write longer and more detailed literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently using appropriate text organization and growing understanding of register.
Write short literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently.
Write longer literary and informational texts (e.g., an argument for protecting the rainforests) collaboratively (e.g., with peers) and independently using appropriate text organization.

Apply increasing understanding of how ideas, events, or reasons are linked throughout a text using an increasing variety of academic connecting and transitional words or phrases (e.g., consequently, specifically, however, moreover) to comprehending texts and writing cohesive texts.

Expand noun phrases in an increasing variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative and general academic adjectives to noun phrases or more complex clause embedding) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.
Expand noun phrases in simple ways (e.g., adding a sensory adjective to a noun) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.
